# Brakes Bleed and Master Cylinder Replaced, Still Going to Floor

When you've swapped the master cylinder and bled the system multiple times, yet the pedal remains soft or goes all the way to the floor, you are no longer dealing with a simple air issue. You have systematically ruled out the two most common culprits in hydraulic brake systems. At this stage, the problem has shifted from "air in the lines" or "failed seals inside the master cylinder" to either a mechanical disconnect, a catastrophic seal failure within the wheel cylinders or calipers, or a compromised hydraulic path that bypasses pressure entirely.

The first thing to verify is the physical connection between the pedal and the master cylinder. A very common oversight occurs when the pushrod height is incorrect after installing a new unit. If the pushrod does not make full contact with the piston inside the master cylinder bore, or if it bottoms out prematurely due to improper adjustment, you can have a perfectly good master cylinder that mechanically cannot build pressure. The pedal will travel through the entire stroke of the master cylinder body without ever transferring force to the fluid. Before assuming internal failure, physically measure the pushrod extension against the manufacturer's specifications for your specific vehicle model. If the rod is too long or the mounting bracket has shifted, the hydraulic circuit is mechanically open before it even starts.

If the mechanical linkage is solid, you must consider the integrity of the wheel-end components. Even if you bled the brakes recently, air can enter the system again immediately if there is a leaking seal on a caliper piston or a wheel cylinder cup that hasn't been addressed. A failing rubber seal allows fluid to bypass internally rather than building pressure against the brake pads or shoes. When you pump the pedal, the master cylinder pushes fluid into the line, but the high-pressure side of the wheel cylinder leaks back toward the low-pressure reservoir side through the worn seal. This creates a "soft" pedal that eventually bottoms out because there is no resistance to build pressure.

To diagnose this, perform a bench test on the suspect caliper or wheel cylinder if you can isolate them. With the brake lines disconnected and the bleeder valve closed, try to pressurize the unit with fluid from a reservoir while holding it up to observe for leaks. If fluid sprays out of the back of the piston or seeps around the seal when pressure is applied, that component must be replaced. It is not enough to just tighten the mounting bolts; the internal hydraulic integrity is compromised.

Another potential pitfall involves the proportioning valve or the brake booster itself. If the vacuum diaphragm inside the booster has failed, the master cylinder might still function mechanically, but the assist will feel like there is no fluid pressure because the force isn't being applied to the piston face. Similarly, a blocked internal passage in the proportioning valve can cause one side of the brakes to work while the other feels dead, leading to a pedal that sinks if you are testing on the disabled side.

Finally, ensure your brake fluid is not contaminated with moisture or glycol from old coolant leaks. Glycol-based brake fluids react violently with moisture, turning into an acidic sludge that eats away at seals and lowers the boiling point of the entire system. If you haven't flushed the fluid recently, or if there was a coolant leak that you missed during the bleeding process, the fluid properties themselves might be preventing proper hydraulic transfer. Replace the fluid and inspect all lines for corrosion or swelling before reassembling.
